newsitem.title: USA: U.S. may get lion's share of Pakistan wheat tender.
newsitem.headline: U.S. may get lion's share of Pakistan wheat tender.

text.p: The United States could get the lion's share of this weekend's expanded Pakistani wheat tender because Australia may be unable to sell more nearby wheat, U.S. exporters and traders said.
"It will be all U.S. and for 450,000 tonnes," a wheat trader on the Chicago Board of Trade said.
On Thursday, Pakistan amended its side-by-side U.S. and Australian wheat tenders to 450,000 tonnes each from 360,000 tonnes, its U.S. export agent said.
The tender was scheduled for February 16.
The delivery dates were also changed to February 25-March 31 for both tenders, from the originally announced March 5-31.
Since November, Pakistan has issued side-by-side monthly tenders for Australian and U.S. wheat, its U.S. export agent said.
"Pakistan has tendered for 450,000 tonnes basis U.S. wheat and 450,000 tonnes, basis Australian wheat," the agent said.

"But normally they only purchase one total of those tenders. Sometimes they may buy all the quantity from Australia and sometimes they buy all the wheat from the U.S. and sometimes they will mix it," the agent said.
"It could go to the U.S. It's possible," another wheat trader said. But U.S. wheat compared to other origins was still expensive.
"The bottom line is, it may be some spot business, but it doesn't change the overall dynamics," said Mickey Luth, director of research for the LaiFa Group.
He said U.S. wheat is still high-priced relative to other origins.
Once Canada corrects its shipping problems, which may be in about 60 days, Luth said he expected wheat buyers to go there rather than to the U.S.
On February 5, Australian Wheat Board chairman Trevor Flugge said the board had full orders for months ahead and was unable to sell more wheat in nearby months.
The AWB had not sold out of Australian Standard White (ASW) but had reached the point where it had sold enough that it was now looking at the quality end of the market, Flugge said.

One U.S. exporter said there seems to be a lot of talk the Australians were probably close to stressing their capacity for March shipment although they sold 37,000 tonnes of wheat for March to the Japanese Food Agency on Wednesday.
Yet another exporter added: "I think the Australians (would) prefer the upcoming Indian business because that is cash and Pakistan would involve credit."
But a third exporter said the situation was still not clear. "I don't see anything whether the Australian wheat board will offer or not," the exporter said.
